passage: In the lobby of the accounts firm, a man in a creased shirt caught Hemant by the elbow: his wallet had been stolen, and he needed cash for a bus to Nagpur. Hemant's chest tightened. Only last month a colleague had lost money to a story much like this one. And Hemant could not be sure the man was lying. "I'm sorry, I don't hand out cash," Hemant said, "but I can help another way." Hemant turned to Omkar, the security guard. "Can you call the police help desk and ask what they do for stranded travellers?" Omkar nodded and picked up the phone. Hemant walked to the canteen and came back with a packet of poha and tea. The man took it, said thanks and sat down to wait. Hemant went upstairs unsure whether it was enough, but at peace with it.

qa.q: What did Hemant bring back from the canteen?
qa.a: Hemant brought back a packet of poha and tea.

qa.q: Why did Hemant's chest tighten when the man asked for cash?
qa.a: Hemant remembered a colleague losing money to a similar story, so felt fear of being scammed, though Hemant could not be sure the man was lying.

qa.q: How did Hemant offer help while staying cautious?
qa.a: Hemant declined to hand over cash, asked Omkar to call the police help desk, and bought food and tea instead.

qa.q: How might the man in the creased shirt see Hemant's refusal of cash?
qa.a: He may be disappointed, but the food and the phone call may show him that the refusal was caution, not coldness.

grounding: A stranger asks Hemant for money; Hemant hesitates because of scams, acts on caution, and offers safe help such as a call to the police help desk and food.

passage:
So, Pallavi, you asked why I went quiet in the car on Friday. Okay.
There was this man at the petrol pump near the flyover. Clean shirt, bag on his shoulder. 'Behenji,' he said, his wallet was stolen and he needed money for a bus to Nashik. And my whole body went stiff. My brother got taken by exactly that story last year, the same sad face, the same bus.
Part of me wanted to just drive off. Part of me thought, what if it's true?
So I did the middle thing. I said, 'I'm Nikita, I won't give cash, but I can buy you a meal from that stall, and there's a police booth right there if you need help getting home.'
He took the vada pav, didn't go to the booth. I still don't know if he was honest. I felt mean and sensible at the same time.

qa.q: What did the man at the petrol pump say he needed money for?
qa.a: 'Behenji,' he said, his wallet was stolen and he needed money for a bus to Nashik.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when the man asked for money?
qa.a: She felt afraid and torn, stiff with the memory of her brother being tricked, yet worried the man's story might be true.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Nikita, and why?
qa.a: Buying him a meal and pointing to the police booth let her help safely without handing over cash, so she respected her caution and still stayed kind.

qa.q: How might the man have seen Nikita's offer?
qa.a: If his story was true, he may have felt some relief at the food but frustrated not to get bus fare; if it was not, her offer quietly left him nothing to exploit.

grounding: A young woman hesitates when a stranger asks for money because she fears a scam, and chooses safe help that honours her instinct without making her hard-hearted.

passage:
Monday: Jyoti was locking her scooter outside the office at nine at night when a woman asked for a lift to the hospital. Jyoti said 'sorry, no' and rode off fast, heart pounding. She couldn't sleep, wondering if the woman had been in real trouble.
Wednesday: At lunch she told Chaitanya. He listened and said, 'You weren't wrong to be careful at night. But you could have called an auto or the helpline for her. That's still help.' Jyoti saved the city helpline and the nearest auto stand number in her phone.
Saturday: An old man outside the metro asked her for money for medicine. Her stomach tightened again. This time she walked him to the pharmacy counter and asked the chemist to help him, then showed him the station help desk. He blessed her twice. She went home steadier.

qa.q: What did Jyoti save in her phone on Wednesday?
qa.a: She saved the city helpline and the nearest auto stand number.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel after refusing the woman on Monday night?
qa.a: She felt guilty and restless; she could not sleep, wondering if the woman had been in real trouble.

qa.q: What changed in how Jyoti responded between Monday and Saturday?
qa.a: On Monday she only refused, but by Saturday she kept her caution and still helped safely by taking the man to the pharmacy counter and the station help desk.

qa.q: How might the old man outside the metro have seen Jyoti's help?
qa.a: He likely felt grateful and respected, since she did not wave him away but made sure someone could actually help him; he blessed her twice.

grounding: Over a week a young woman moves from fearful refusal to safe, practical help for strangers, trusting her caution without becoming hard-hearted.
